slides.headline: Is my pain actually sciatica?
slides.body: Sciatica has become the catch-all label for any back-and-leg pain. Most of what gets called sciatica is something else. Here is the diagnostic pattern I use before the label gets stuck.

slides.headline: The label decides the treatment.
slides.body: Sciatica gets treated as a nerve case. Piriformis syndrome gets treated as a muscle case. Same leg pain, very different plan. If the label is wrong, the treatment chases the wrong tissue and the pain hangs around.

slides.headline: Actual sciatica follows a very specific pattern.
slides.body: It starts at the low back. It runs down the hip, across the outside of the shin, and through the ankle. The whole path. If your pain skips a section, it is more likely piriformis syndrome.
slides.quoteText: Actual diagnosis of sciatica is a very specific pattern — starts at the low back, runs down the hip, across the outside of the shin and through the ankle. If your pain doesn't follow that full pattern, it's more likely piriformis syndrome.

slides.headline: Trace it head to foot.
slides.body: Sciatica follows the full path. If your symptoms hit one piece and skip the rest, the conversation shifts to the piriformis.
slides.diagramConnector: Full path = sciatica. Partial path = look at the piriformis.

slides.headline: If the path is partial, look at the piriformis.
slides.body: Piriformis syndrome reproduces leg pain when a deep hip muscle compresses the nerve locally. The pain stays around the glute and back of the thigh, and it does not run the full sciatic line down to the ankle.
slides.quoteText: Local glute and back-of-thigh pain that stops short of the full sciatic path is usually piriformis. Treat the muscle, calm the nerve.

slides.headline: Three questions to ask first.
slides.body: Where does the pain start? Where does it stop? Does it run the full path or only a section? Those three readouts get you most of the way to a useful working diagnosis before anyone says the word sciatica.
slides.goldAccent: The label that travels with you decides the plan that gets built. Get the label right.

slides.body: If you have been told you have sciatica and the plan has not moved the pain, send me a DM and let's trace the actual path together.
slides.tagline: Your threshold is higher than they told you.

caption:
Is my pain actually sciatica? It is one of the most common questions I get, and most of what gets called sciatica turns out to be something else.

Actual sciatica is a specific pattern. It starts at the low back. It runs down the hip, across the outside of the shin, and through the ankle. The whole path. If your pain skips a section, it is more likely piriformis syndrome.

The label decides the plan. Sciatica gets treated as a nerve case. Piriformis syndrome gets treated as a muscle case. Same leg pain, very different treatment.

Before you self-label, ask three questions. Where does the pain start. Where does it stop. Does it run the full path or only a section. Those three readouts get you most of the way to a useful working diagnosis.

If you have been told you have sciatica and the plan has not moved the pain, send me a DM and let's trace the actual path together.
